questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Bending in a stone lintel
questions.learningObjective: state the load a spanning lintel resists and why that fixes its span
questions.stem: A doorway is cut from limestone: two uprights carry a single long stone across the opening. What is that lintel actually resisting, and why does the answer fix how wide the opening can be?

options.text: Bending: the lintel sags between its supports, putting its underside in tension, and stone cracks across there
Pure compression: the lintel is squeezed from end to end, exactly as a wedge in an arch would be
options.misconception: believes the lintel is squeezed end to end like a voussoir, confusing a bending member with a compression ring

options.text: Shear: the lintel is being sliced through its depth by the downward pull of its own weight
options.misconception: treats the lintel as sliced in shear, confusing the weight carried with a force acting across the section

options.text: Tension alone: the lintel hangs from the two posts, which act like a pair of suspenders holding it
options.misconception: thinks the posts hold the lintel up like suspenders, so the stone would be in pure tension the whole length

questions.explanation: A member held at both ends and loaded along its length bends, and bending puts the top of the section in compression and the bottom in tension. Stone is strong in compression and very weak in tension, so the crack always begins on the underside and runs across. The bending moment at midspan grows with the square of the span, which is why a limestone lintel serves short openings only; a wider opening needs a deeper member or a longer stone, and long stones are hard to quarry and to move. That is the reason builders who wanted width reached for the arch, which works in compression all the way round its ring.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the underside of a long stone when its ends are held up and its middle is heavy.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why an arch outlives a lintel
questions.learningObjective: explain why an arch spans further than a lintel of the same opening
questions.stem: A builder wants an eight-metre opening in stone, with no metal available. Compare one long stone lintel with a semicircular arch of many small blocks. Why is the arch the workable answer?

options.text: The arch turns the load into compression along its wedge blocks and delivers it as inclined thrust to the supports
The arch is lighter in total, so the same foundations can carry a wider opening than a solid lintel
options.misconception: assumes the arch is lighter than the lintel it replaces, mistaking a change of force path for a change of mass

options.text: The arch needs no support while it is raised, so it can be built over an opening that is already finished
options.misconception: believes a true arch needs no temporary support while it is raised, forgetting the timber centring

options.text: The arch takes the load off the piers altogether, since the ring floats free in the space between them
options.misconception: thinks an arch floats free of its supports and relieves them of load instead of loading them with thrust

questions.explanation: An arch is a ring of wedge-shaped blocks that are squeezed against one another, and masonry is strongest exactly there, in compression. Because the load can travel through a compression ring, the opening can be wide while the individual stones stay small enough to quarry and to lift. The load is not abolished: it leaves the ring as an inclined thrust at each springing, so the supports must be broad and heavy enough to take it. A lintel fails in tension at the same width, and a full ring still needs a temporary centre until the crown is closed.
questions.hint: Ask which way the force travels inside a ring of wedge-shaped stones, and which way it leaves at the bottom.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The keystone in the ring
questions.learningObjective: state what the keystone does for a masonry arch
questions.stem: A stone arch is finished with a single wedge-shaped block set last, at the crown, its outward face carved with a relief. What does that block do for the structure?

options.text: It locks the ring: until the last joint is wedged tight, the blocks can slide outward and the arch cannot stand
It carries the entire weight of the arch by itself, with every other stone acting only as a filler beside it
options.misconception: believes the keystone alone bears the arch's weight, not knowing the ring shares it in compression

options.text: It is a decorated panel that could be lifted out tomorrow without changing how the arch behaves at all
options.misconception: thinks the carved block is decoration that can be removed with no structural consequence at all

options.text: It ties the two springings together, working as a horizontal tie against the arch's outward push
options.misconception: confuses an arch with a beam, assuming masonry needs a tie across the opening against its push

questions.explanation: A ring of voussoirs is held in place by the mutual pressure of its neighbours, and that pressure cannot be established while a gap remains at the crown. The keystone is the block that closes the last joint, wedges the two halves of the ring against each other and transfers the load through the crown, where the two inclined thrusts of the halves balance. That is also why the centring can be struck once it is set. A well-built arch carries its load in compression only, so it needs no tie across the opening: a tie is a remedy for a straight beam, not for an arch.
questions.hint: Ask what the ring cannot do while there is still a gap in it at the top.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the blocks are wedges
questions.learningObjective: explain what the wedge shape of a voussoir does to the load path
questions.stem: In a cut-stone arch each block is wider at the outer face than at the inner one, and the joints between blocks all point towards the centre. What follows from that geometry for how the arch works?

options.text: Each block is squeezed between its neighbours, so the ring carries load in compression and the joints stay shut
Each block can slide along its neighbour, which is what lets an arch adjust itself to any settlement
options.misconception: believes the wedges can slide along each other, so the ring hinges instead of locking under pressure

options.text: The joints point at the centre only as a setting-out guide, with no effect on how the load travels
options.misconception: reads the radiating joints as a mason's layout mark with no structural function whatever

options.text: The wedge shape lets each block carry load in tension, so the ring can bridge a gap wider than a lintel
options.misconception: thinks a wedge-shaped stone resists being pulled apart, reversing what compression does for masonry

questions.explanation: The joints are radial because the line of thrust through the arch runs across them at right angles. That is what keeps every joint closed and every block in compression: the stone ahead pushes back, so the ring cannot hinge open at any joint. A ring with joints running the other way would have nothing holding it together except friction and would slump as it settled. Tearing the blocks apart in tension is the one thing an arch must never ask of stone, and the wedge shape is precisely the geometry that avoids asking for it.
questions.hint: Ask which direction the force travels inside the ring, and therefore how a joint should be cut.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a pier under a vault must resist
questions.learningObjective: identify the force a vault delivers to the pier beneath it
questions.stem: A stone barrel vault is carried on a free-standing pier at the springing line, with a lower aisle beyond that pier. What has the builder had to check about the pier itself?

options.text: The outward push the vault makes where it springs, and whether the pier's mass and footing can hold against it
Only the weight of the vault above, because a masonry vault presses straight down and never sideways
options.misconception: treats a vault as a lid pressing straight down, forgetting that a barrel arches sideways at its ends

options.text: The height of the aisle roof, so that rain running off the vault drains onto the top of the pier
options.misconception: thinks the pier's job is to catch rainwater from the vault, a job the aisle roof already does

options.text: The span of the vault, on the assumption that a wider span always wants a taller pier rather than a broader one
options.misconception: believes span is met by making piers taller rather than broader, height being no help against overturning

questions.explanation: A vault is a barrel that has been extended in both directions, and a barrel behaves like a continuous arch: at each springing it delivers a force that is inclined outward as well as downward. The pier therefore has to be heavy and splayed enough that this thrust neither overturns it nor slides its base, which is why medieval piers are broad, battered and often buttressed further downstream. Treating the vault as a heavy lid that only presses down is the standard misreading, and it is why so many drawings of vaulted interiors show supports far too slender for the loads they carry.
questions.hint: Ask what a long barrel does at its ends, and in which direction that force travels there.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The load path of a ribbed vault
questions.learningObjective: explain what a ribbed vault changes about where the load is delivered
questions.stem: A stone ceiling is built as a framework of diagonal ribs with thin curved panels slung between them, the ribs carried down onto piers at the corners. What does that arrangement buy over a plain barrel vault of the same span?

options.text: The ribs gather the ceiling's weight into a few points, so the supports can be discrete piers and the wall between them freed
The whole ceiling becomes much lighter, since thin panels replace the solid mass a barrel vault would require
options.misconception: concludes the ceiling is lighter because the panels are thin, missing that the ribs grew to take their load

options.text: The thrust is taken clean out of the building, so no external buttressing is needed on the outside at all
options.misconception: believes ribbing removes the thrust from the building, so exterior buttressing becomes unnecessary

options.text: The panels can be made of glass, so the vault lights the space below without any change in its structure
options.misconception: assumes the webs can be glazed, treating a structural vault web as a window opening

questions.explanation: In a ribbed vault the thin webs span only from rib to rib, and the ribs, built up in several courses of squared stone, collect that load and deliver it as concentrated thrusts to named points. Because the load now arrives at points rather than continuously, the wall between them no longer has to be a load-bearing mass and can be opened for windows. The thrust is not gone, only relocated: it still has to be carried, which is why the external supports appear at the same time as the ribs. Lightness and glass are attractive answers and neither is the structural change.
questions.hint: Ask where the load is collected, and how many places actually receive it at the bottom.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the wall can be opened up
questions.learningObjective: explain how a wall pierced with large windows can still carry a vault
questions.stem: A survey of a medieval church records windows with far more glazed area than solid wall left standing between them, the glass held in slender bars of cut stone. What has made that possible?

options.text: The vault's outward thrust is carried past the wall by external supports, so the wall is a fill rather than a mass
The masons used thinner stone, because a thin wall is always lighter and therefore always the stronger choice
options.misconception: believes thin stone is stronger than thick stone, reversing what a bearing wall's thickness does

options.text: The glass itself is structural, since a sheet of coloured glass can take a thrust as well as a stone pier can
options.misconception: treats the glazing as structural, forgetting that bars and mullions carry the glass's weight

options.text: The wall was built as two thin skins around a hollow core, so the vault loads pass through the cavity below
options.misconception: imagines a hollow-cored wall, a modern construction detail that gives a bearing wall no strength at all

questions.explanation: Where a vault has to be carried inside the building, the wall must be a load-bearing mass, and its thickness is a structural requirement rather than a preference: that is why early vaulted churches have few, small, deeply splayed windows. Take the thrust out of the wall and the wall becomes a windscreen. It can then be thinned and pierced, and the stone bars and mullions carry the weight of the glass and the pressure of wind on it. Glass is never a support, and a hollow core has no structural purpose in a bearing wall.
questions.hint: Ask where the vault's sideways push is being taken, and what that frees the wall to do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The force a flying buttress takes
questions.learningObjective: trace the load path through a flying buttress
questions.stem: An arched prop rises from outside the building, passes over the roof of the aisle, and lands against the upper haunch of the high vault. Which force is it dealing with, and where does that force end up?

options.text: The vault's outward thrust, caught high up and carried over the aisle to a heavier outer pier and down
The weight of the aisle roof, so that the aisle can be vaulted instead of being covered in timber
options.misconception: reads the flyer as a prop for the aisle roof, confusing a thrust catcher with a vertical support

options.text: Wind pressure on the upper wall, which would otherwise blow the clerestory inwards during a storm
options.misconception: credits the flyer with resisting wind rather than with the vault's sideways thrust

options.text: The vault's weight, which the prop carries straight down through the aisle wall into the foundations
options.misconception: believes the flyer carries the vault's weight straight down, ignoring the outward component of the thrust

questions.explanation: A ribbed vault pushes outward and downward at its haunches, and the flyer is a half-arch placed to meet it there, above the roof of the aisle. The prop passes the force outward to a separate, massive buttress pier, and from there it goes down through the pier's own weight into the foundations. Everything in between is left free: the aisle roof can be a lean-to against the wall, and the wall at the springing level is not asked to resist anything. Confusing the flyer with a vertical prop, or crediting it with resisting wind, is the standard error.
questions.hint: Ask what a vault does at its haunches, and follow that force outwards to where it can be absorbed.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a tensioned concrete beam spans further
questions.learningObjective: explain what post-tensioning does to the stress in a concrete beam
questions.stem: A concrete beam is cast first, and steel tendons are threaded through it afterwards and pulled tight with a jack. Why does that beam carry more load than the same beam cast with those tendons left slack?

options.text: Tensioning puts the beam's underside into compression, cancelling the flexural tension that would crack concrete
The tendons make the concrete itself harder, so the same section resists more load than it did before
options.misconception: thinks the tendons somehow harden the concrete, confusing prestressing with a stronger material

options.text: The tendons take the whole weight of the beam in pure tension, leaving the concrete to carry nothing at all
options.misconception: believes the steel takes the whole load alone, leaving the concrete section doing no work at all

options.text: The jack preloads the supports, so the beam barely bends and the path of the load hardly matters
options.misconception: thinks jacking the supports removes bending altogether, which is not what prestressing does

questions.explanation: Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension, and a plain beam fails by cracking on the face that is pulled apart. Prestressing puts the whole section into compression before any service load arrives, so when the load tries to open a crack on the underside it is working against a compression that is already there. A much shallower section can then carry the same span, and post-tensioning allows the tendons to be threaded after the concrete has hardened. The tendons are steel and can take tension; the gain belongs to the combination, not to any change in the concrete.
questions.hint: Ask which face of a loaded beam is pulled apart, and what that face is doing before the load arrives.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a column has base, shaft and capital
questions.learningObjective: explain the structural job performed by each part of a column
questions.stem: A stone column is described as having a base, a shaft and a capital. Why is the member divided into those three parts rather than left as one plain cylinder standing on the floor?

options.text: Each part has a job: the base spreads the load, the shaft carries it, the capital widens to receive what sits above
The divisions are a matter of the order's style, with no structural difference standing behind any of them
options.misconception: reads the divisions as stylistic convention with no change of structural condition behind them

options.text: The shaft is hollow to save weight, so the base and the capital simply close off the tube at either end
options.misconception: believes the shaft is a hollow tube, so base and capital are just end pieces of it

options.text: The capital is the only part that touches the floor, so the base and shaft are ornamental reversals of it
options.misconception: thinks the capital carries the load into the floor, reversing the direction of the load path

questions.explanation: A column is a load path with three changes of condition in it. At the foot the load leaves the member and enters the floor, so the base spreads it over a wider area and stops the toe of the shaft from sliding. Through the shaft the load is axial, which is the one direction stone handles perfectly. At the head the load passes from a round section into the square section of an entablature, or into the springing of an arch, so the capital widens and distributes it. The divisions mark those conditions exactly, which is why the ornament concentrates there.
questions.hint: Ask what the load is doing at the foot, in the middle and at the head of the member.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What distinguishes the three classical orders
questions.learningObjective: state what separates the classical column orders from one another
questions.stem: Three column orders are compared: one has no base and a plain cushion-shaped capital, one has scrolls on its capital, one has carved leaves. Which statement about the three is right?

options.text: They differ in proportion and in the treatment of base and capital, and each is named after a Greek city
They are three stages of a historical sequence, each order built to replace the one before it in practice
options.misconception: believes the orders are a progress from simple to refined, each replacing the one before it

options.text: They are three heights of one column, differing only in the number of drums stacked in the shaft
options.misconception: thinks the orders are simply three sizes of one column, differing in the number of drums

options.text: Each order was used for one particular temple and was never repeated anywhere else in the ancient world
options.misconception: believes each order belongs to a single named temple and was never used again elsewhere

questions.explanation: The orders are conventions of proportion and detailing. The baseless order with the plain capital is the Doric, the scrolled capital belongs to the Ionic, and the leaf-carved capital to the Corinthian, and the names come from the Greek cities whose temples were credited with them. They coexisted instead of succeeding one another, and architects mixed them freely, so an order is evidence of a design vocabulary rather than of a date. Reading an order as a fixed building type, or as a simple change of size, is what makes elevations hard to measure against each other.
questions.hint: Ask what the names refer to, and whether one order ever displaced another in practice.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A colonnade on three sides
questions.learningObjective: identify a peripteral temple plan and its consequence
questions.stem: A temple plan shows a walled cella wrapped on three sides by a free-standing colonnade, with a porch in front and a blank wall closing the rear. Which description of the design fits that plan?

options.text: A peripteral scheme, composed to be looked at and walked around from outside rather than entered from one side only
A single frontal scheme, with columns engaged against the cella wall and one privileged doorway
options.misconception: mistakes columns engaged against the wall for a free-standing colonnade on three sides

options.text: A basilican scheme, with the cella divided into a tall nave and lower side aisles for an assembly
options.misconception: reads the cella as an aisled hall, confusing a single room with a basilica's nave and aisles

options.text: A domed scheme, with the cella acting as the square bay that carries a vault on four pendentives
options.misconception: imagines a square bay carrying a vault, which is a different structural problem altogether

questions.explanation: A free-standing colonnade running down both flanks and across the rear is what makes the plan peripteral, and the consequence is that the building is composed for the view from outside: the same order, spacing and entablature face every direction, and the walled cella inside stays relatively small. The entrance is a porch on one short side, but the architecture does not stop at that door. A colonnade engaged against the cella wall, or a single dominant front, belongs to another tradition, and an aisled or domed hall answers a different question altogether.
questions.hint: Ask how many sides the colonnade stands free on, and what that does to the building's viewing conditions.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a podium and a single stair achieve
questions.learningObjective: infer what a raised podium and one stair do to a temple's approach and structure
questions.stem: A temple stands on a high platform with one wide staircase at the front and no steps at all on the other three sides. What does that arrangement achieve?

options.text: It concentrates the approach on a single axis, and it lets the cella be vaulted because the platform can take the loads
It makes the building defensible, since a raised platform with one approach is the safest plan to hold
options.misconception: reads the podium as fortification, importing a modern military logic into an ancient plan

options.text: It shortens the columns, because the stylobate can be laid on fill instead of on the natural rock
options.misconception: believes a raised stylobate shortens the columns, when platform height changes no column proportion

options.text: It provides a market around the building, so the surrounding colonnade becomes a covered walk for traders
options.misconception: thinks the colonnade is a covered market walk, ignoring that the single stair controls the access

questions.explanation: A podium lifts the whole building clear of its surroundings and leaves one front as the only way in, which concentrates both the ritual and the visual approach on a single axis. It also solves a structural problem: standing on a platform, a cella can be roofed with concrete vaults carried on piers, so the interior can be far larger and the front can read as a screen of columns rather than as a wall. The defensive reading is a modern reflex imported into an ancient plan, and the trading reading ignores that the stair, not the perimeter, is the controlled route.
questions.hint: Ask how many directions of approach survive, and what a platform lets the interior walls be replaced with.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the pediment closes
questions.learningObjective: state the compositional function of a pediment
questions.stem: A triangular gable sits above the entablature, its two raking cornices following the slope of the roof behind it. What does the pediment do for the design of the front?

options.text: It closes the front as one bounded, symmetrical composition, and its triangle gives sculpture a place to go
It hides the timber of the roof, which was never meant to be seen from the ground in front of it
options.misconception: believes the pediment exists to hide the roof structure from anyone standing in front of it

options.text: It throws rainwater clear of the facade, so the front wall is kept dry during a storm
options.misconception: treats the pediment as rainwater shedding, which is a side effect of a framed composition

options.text: It opens the front, since the empty triangle lets daylight from the porch reach into the cella
options.misconception: imagines an open pediment admitting light, confusing a later variant with the closed type

questions.explanation: The pediment terminates the whole elevation: the entablature runs across, the cornices turn up at the corners, and the result reads as a figure with a base, a middle and a head. That enclosure is what makes a classical front a single composition rather than a wall with a roof sitting on it. The enclosed triangular field is the tympanum, the most legible surface on the building, which is why sculpture goes there. Shedding water and covering structure are real but incidental functions here, and an open pediment is a later variant rather than the starting point.
questions.hint: Ask what a bounded triangle does to a long horizontal composition, and where it leaves room to carve.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a triangle constrains a figure group
questions.learningObjective: infer how the shape of a tympanum limits a sculptural composition
questions.stem: A pediment's triangular field is filled with a row of figures carved at a single scale along its base, the field narrowing to a point above them. How does the shape of the field govern that composition?

options.text: The usable width falls away as the field rises, so figures placed higher must be smaller, and only the base is a wide register
The triangle has no effect at all, since a sculptor may cut any figure at any size at any height in it
options.misconception: believes a triangular field places no limit on scale, treating a frame as though it were a wall

options.text: The field is square in the original form, and the triangle was added later simply to fit the roof above
options.misconception: thinks the tympanum was originally a square panel and the triangle a later addition

options.text: The field can only be carved in relief, because a figure carved in the round could never be fitted inside it
options.misconception: believes carving in the round is impossible in a pediment, confusing depth with width

questions.explanation: A tympanum is not a rectangle with a pointed top: the usable area collapses as you climb, so a group at one scale fits only along the base and anything higher has to shrink. That is why pedimental sculpture is built as a wide, low band of figures with smaller ones rising towards the apex, and why the composition reads as a frieze inside a frame. A frame constrains, and the misreading that treats the field as a free wall is what produces designs that could never have been carved, let alone stood up.
questions.hint: Ask how wide the field is at a given height, and what that does to a figure of fixed size.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a basilica plan is for
questions.learningObjective: identify a basilica plan and connect its parts to the assembly it serves
questions.stem: A rectangular hall has a tall central space flanked by lower side aisles, a row of clerestory windows above the aisle roofs, and an apse closing the far end. What kind of plan is that, and what was such a building for?

options.text: A basilica plan: an aisled longitudinal hall made for an assembly, and later for a congregation facing the altar
A domed central-plan hall, made for a gathered group with no directional emphasis of any kind
options.misconception: confuses a domed central-plan hall with a longitudinal aisled hall built for an audience

options.text: A temple plan with a colonnade all round, made so that the building could be walked around on every side
options.misconception: reads the clerestory as evidence of a colonnade running round the outside of the building

options.text: A palace plan of rooms around a courtyard, made for a household rather than for any congregation
options.misconception: takes an apse for a courtyard, confusing a ritual focus with rooms gathered round a court

questions.explanation: Three features define it: a longitudinal axis, side aisles, and a clerestory that lights the central space from above the lower aisle roofs. The form descends from the large covered hall used for law courts and commerce, and early Christian builders kept the plan because it is built for a crowd that must all see one end, the apse, and the altar within it. The nave holds the congregation, the aisles take overflow and circulation, and the sequence of rising heights is what makes the focus legible from the back of a full hall.
questions.hint: Ask where the light comes from, which way the hall runs, and what stands at the far end of it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a dome needs at its base
questions.learningObjective: state the support condition a hemispherical dome requires at its base
questions.stem: A dome is described as a hemisphere turned about a vertical axis and set on a circular base. What has to be true of that base for the dome to stand at all?

options.text: It must be a continuous ring able to take the compression the shell develops all the way round its own base
Nothing in particular, because a dome shell carries its own weight and needs no support wherever it lands
options.misconception: believes a dome shell is self-supporting, forgetting the ring of thrust at its own base

options.text: It must be dead level, so that the shell does not lean, and the rest of the support is incidental
options.misconception: thinks only the levelness of the base matters, and that shape and ring are unimportant

options.text: It must be wider than the dome's diameter, so the shell cannot slide off the top of the supporting drum
options.misconception: believes the base must outsize the dome, confusing a support ring with a weather-shedding batter

questions.explanation: The geometry settles it. A hemisphere is generated by rotating an arc about a vertical axis, and the weight of the shell runs down the curve to the base, where it becomes a force acting round the circle in every direction at once. That circumferential thrust must be received by something continuous, so a dome is only as sound as the ring it closes onto, whether that ring is carried on a drum, on pendentives or on squinches. This is why a dome is never merely a roof: it is a compression ring that needs a compression ring beneath it.
questions.hint: Ask what the weight of a turning curve becomes when it arrives at the bottom of the turn.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two ways to set a dome over a square
questions.learningObjective: distinguish pendentives from squinches as corner transitions
questions.stem: One building carries a circular dome on four curved triangular sections of masonry filling the upper corners of a square bay. Another fills those corners with small arches to make an octagon. What is the difference between the two?

options.text: The first uses pendentives, which curve continuously from square to circle; the second uses squinches, which step the transition
The first is a Romanesque solution and the second a Gothic one, so the difference is one of period and nothing else
options.misconception: dates the two corner treatments to different periods, treating a technical name as a chronology

options.text: The first is a dome on a drum and the second is a dome without one, so the difference lies in the base ring
options.misconception: confuses a drum with pendentives, since both stand between a dome and the walls below

options.text: There is no difference, since both are ways of closing the corners and the two terms are interchangeable
options.misconception: assumes the two terms are synonyms, as though one word could name two constructions

questions.explanation: Both do the same work, turning a square bay into something that can carry a circle, and the difference is geometrical. Pendentives are four spherical triangles whose curves run continuously from the sides of the square up to the circle of the dome, so the load is gathered smoothly along the four arches below. Squinches build small arches or corbelled masses across each corner, so the square first becomes an octagon and the octagon then receives the circle. One is a curve and the other a set of steps, which is a real construction difference and not a difference of vocabulary.
questions.hint: Ask what shape the four corners become in each case, and whether the change is curved or stepped.

questions.topic: What the drum under a dome buys
questions.learningObjective: explain what raising a dome's springing on a drum allows
questions.stem: A dome is raised on a cylindrical drum ringed with tall windows instead of springing straight from the corners of the square bay below it. What problem does putting it up on the drum solve?

It makes the dome itself lighter, since a smaller shell always needs a taller drum than a broad one would
options.misconception: thinks a raised springing lightens the shell, reversing the effect of a larger base ring

options.text: It permits a wider span below, because the drum spreads the dome's weight evenly across the whole bay
options.misconception: believes the drum spreads the dome's weight sideways and so widens the span below it

options.text: It removes the need for pendentives or squinches, since the drum carries the circle directly down to the floor
options.misconception: thinks a drum replaces the corner transition, forgetting pendentives or squinches still work below it

questions.explanation: A dome that springs low has its base ring at the level of the bay's corners, which is exactly where windows would have to be. Lifting the springing on a drum puts the base ring above the heads of the openings, so the drum can be a whole storey of windows lighting the space below, and the wall under it is left free of tall holes. The drum does not spread the load sideways, does not lighten the shell, and is independent of the corner transition, which still has to be done below by pendentives or squinches.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The structural difference between two churches
questions.learningObjective: compare Romanesque and Gothic construction by where the load is carried
questions.stem: One church has barrel or groin vaults, round arches, few small windows and very thick continuous walls. Another has pointed arches, ribbed vaults, large traceried windows, and slender piers with external supports. What separates them structurally?

options.text: The first carries its vaults on solid wall, so the wall must be thick; the second carries them on ribs and piers and takes the thrust outside
The two differ only in decoration, since the same wall thickness and the same vaulting serve both buildings equally well
options.misconception: believes the two churches differ in decoration only, holding construction to be a matter of taste

options.text: The first is a basilica and the second a domed hall, so the difference lies in the roof over the aisle
options.misconception: reads the difference as a roof type, confusing a vaulted nave with a hall under a dome

options.text: The second is the heavier building, because pointed arches and added ribs weigh more than round arches do
options.misconception: assumes the ribbed and pointed church must be heavier, counting added members as added load

questions.explanation: Everything follows from where the load goes. Vaults and arches deliver a thrust at their springings, so a church that must take that thrust inside its own walls needs massive continuous walls, small openings and solid supports between them. That is the Romanesque condition. Once the load is gathered onto discrete piers by ribs and carried out of the building by flyers, the wall between the piers is no longer a bearing mass and can be thin and almost entirely window. The pointed arch helps at a given span, but the exterior support is what frees the wall.
questions.hint: Ask, for each church, where the vault's sideways push finally has to be absorbed.

questions.topic: The difference between a buttress and a pier
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a buttress from a pier in the vocabulary of support
questions.stem: A building specification names a free-standing pier inside the building and a heavy buttress built against the outside of a wall, and both are working for the same vault. What distinguishes the two?

options.text: The pier is a vertical support that receives the vault's thrust and weight; the buttress adds mass to resist overturning
The buttress is always semicircular in plan and the pier is always rectangular, so shape alone tells them apart
options.misconception: reads buttress and pier as shapes fixed in plan, so every buttress must be round

options.text: The pier is structural while the buttress is ornamental, so a wall with only buttresses carries nothing at all
options.misconception: divides the vocabulary into decorative and structural, so a buttressed wall carries nothing

options.text: There is no difference, since in older buildings the two words are used interchangeably for the same mass
options.misconception: believes the two terms are interchangeable, hiding a real difference in how thrust is resisted

questions.explanation: A pier is a post: a vertical member that receives a thrust at its top and carries it, with its own load, down to the ground. A buttress is a mass, usually an outward thickening of the wall itself, added at the point where the thrust arrives so that the resultant stays inside the base instead of tipping the wall over. That is why buttressing can be applied to a wall after the fact, and why a buttress pier standing free of the building still counts as buttressing rather than as a column. The two words are not interchangeable, and a shape rule explains nothing about either.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two is an independent member and which is extra mass added to something else.

questions.learningObjective: match the parts of a church plan to the liturgical work they serve
questions.stem: A church plan shows a long nave, a transept crossing it near the far end, a choir beyond the crossing, and a passage running behind the high altar. Which set of uses fits those parts?

options.text: The nave holds the congregation, the crossing concentrates the clergy, the choir sings, and the passage lets the altar be reached from behind
The nave is the singers' gallery, the transept is a market, the choir is the vestry, and the passage is a road outside
options.misconception: confuses a choir with a gallery, a market with a transept and a vestry with a passage

options.text: All four parts are identical in use and differ only in size, since medieval churches were planned without differentiated functions
options.misconception: assumes medieval plans had no differentiated functions, so all four parts are interchangeable

options.text: The transept forms the main entrance, so the congregation enters through it and the nave is in fact the choir
options.misconception: believes the transept is the west door, putting the entrance across the axis of the nave

questions.explanation: Each part answers a different requirement. The nave is the volume that holds the laity, and it is made tall and unobstructed for that reason. The crossing, where nave and transept meet, is the place of honour and the focus of movement, and the choir beyond it is where the singers stand. The passage behind the altar is circulation: it lets those who officiate reach the sanctuary without walking down the nave in front of the congregation. questions.topic: The orders applied to a Renaissance palace
questions.learningObjective: explain what a stacked order does for a Renaissance palace front
questions.stem: A palace front is laid out as a grid of equal bays: the ground storey is faced in deeply rusted blocks, and a single order of pilasters runs unbroken from the second storey to the cornice. What has the designer done?

options.text: Stacked a classical order over a heavy base, so the whole front reads as one system rather than as storeys
Copied a temple front exactly, so the palace presents a temple elevation with domestic rooms added behind it
options.misconception: believes the front copies a temple exactly, ignoring the domestic plan behind it

options.text: Doubled the order's height to match the added storeys, so the order grows as tall as the house itself
options.misconception: thinks the order's height is scaled to the storeys, missing that a great order spans them

options.text: Expressed a hierarchy of rooms, with the largest windows left on the ground floor for the daily household
options.misconception: believes the largest windows belong on the ground floor, inverting the hierarchy of the principal floor

questions.explanation: The classical orders are used here as a system of proportion and hierarchy, not as a copy of a building. The rusticated base reads as mass and grounds the front, the great order binds the upper storeys into one continuous vertical rhythm so the elevation is seen as a whole rather than floor by floor, and the regular bay gives the windows a repeatable module. The hierarchy it expresses is a social one, with the principal floor given the best light and the largest openings and the lightest treatment reserved for the top.
questions.hint: Ask what the pilasters do to the way the storeys are read, as opposed to what a temple front would do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The symmetry of a Palladian plan
questions.learningObjective: explain what the fourfold symmetry of a Palladian plan does
questions.stem: A country villa is planned as a square bay with a domed hall in the middle and four identical wings, one on each side, each entered by a two-column portico. What does that symmetry do for the design?

options.text: It fixes the central hall as the hinge of the plan, so the villa can be read and entered from any of the four sides
It maximises the floor area of the wings, since four equal units let each be planned independently of the others
options.misconception: thinks the repeated wings exist to house separate households, missing the compositional point

options.text: It hides the service rooms, since a symmetrical plan by definition pushes every back-of-house space out of sight
options.misconception: believes symmetry is a device for hiding service rooms, which it does not require

options.text: It follows the ground, since a square plan is the only one that can be laid out level on a sloping site
options.misconception: thinks a square plan is chosen because it levels a slope, which geometry cannot do

questions.explanation: The scheme is a dominant central square with four subordinate units repeated about it, and the repetition is what makes the centre legible. Because the wings are equal, no axis is privileged: the building offers four equivalent fronts with their own porticos, and the hall in the middle is what every approach converges on. The classical vocabulary of portico and dome is then applied to a suburban villa, so the plan reads as architecture rather than as a house. Symmetry here is composition, not fortification and not an economy of planning.
questions.hint: Ask what the eye does when four fronts are equal, and which room all four of them lead towards.

questions.learningObjective: infer what a diagonal Baroque axis does to a visitor's experience
questions.stem: A visitor passes through a low, narrow, dim corridor and then emerges into a vast oval hall whose long axis runs across the direction of approach, so nothing is visible straight ahead. What has the plan been arranged to do?

options.text: Stage a change of scale and light as movement, so the space is discovered in stages instead of read at a glance
Fit more people into a given width, since an oval hall encloses more usable floor area than a rectangle does
options.misconception: believes an oval hall is chosen for floor efficiency, confusing sequence with area

options.text: Align the visitor with the far end, since the diagonal axis lines the entrance up with the main doorway
options.misconception: thinks a diagonal axis produces a straight sightline, the opposite of what it denies

options.text: Make the hall work as a market, since a central-plan room with four doors is the shape of a trading floor
options.misconception: reads a central-plan hall as a market, confusing movement of the visitor with the building's use

questions.explanation: The Baroque plan is organised by sequence rather than by a single frontal view. A compressed, dark entry is set against a tall, bright, curved space, and the axis is turned so the visitor must move laterally and round the curve to take the room in. That denies the instant overview a classical hall gives and buys discovery instead, with light and decoration used to direct where the eye goes next. Treating an oval hall as a space-efficiency exercise, or as a market, misses the point of a plan used to govern movement.
questions.hint: Ask what the visitor sees on arrival, and what the turned axis prevents seeing at once.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The frame that made height possible
questions.learningObjective: explain what a steel frame changed about the limit on building height
questions.stem: A twenty-storey building stands on a frame of steel columns and beams, its floors hung inside that frame, and its outer walls reduced to a skin. What is the frame actually doing?

options.text: Carrying the whole building's weight on a small number of points, so height is limited by sway rather than by wall strength
Allowing the building to exceed anything stone could reach, since steel is stronger than stone in every direction at once
options.misconception: believes height is limited only by the strength of the material, ignoring wind sway

options.text: Freeing the walls from the job of support, so they can be replaced entirely by glass and a frame of any height
options.misconception: assumes a frame needs no weather protection, treating the skin as optional

options.text: Eliminating the need for foundations, since the columns themselves transfer every load into the ground below
options.misconception: believes a frame eliminates the need for foundations entirely

questions.explanation: A frame takes the gravity load in concentrated axial forces down a grid of columns, so a wall never has to be a thick bearing mass and the floor loads travel straight to the ground. What the frame cannot do is stop the building from moving sideways: a tall, slender frame acts like a mast, and wind load grows with height and area, so sway and the acceleration it causes become the governing limit. That is why cores, bracing and stiff frames appear as height rises. The frame is not a licence to ignore the wind, and it does not remove the foundations.
questions.hint: Ask which load the columns are sized for, and which load actually decides how high the building can go.

questions.topic: What a curtain wall allows
questions.learningObjective: explain what a hung non-load-bearing wall makes possible
questions.stem: A tower's exterior is a grid of metal panels and glass hung on the outside of the structure and fixed at the top of each panel, the courses overlapping below. What does that arrangement allow?

options.text: All load to be carried by the frame, so the wall can be a thin skin and even one panel can be renewed at a time
The building to be heated by its own walls, since a sealed skin traps warmth inside the frame instead of losing it
options.misconception: treats a sealed skin as a source of heat, confusing an enclosure with a heat source

options.text: The floors to be hung from the skin itself, so that no separate structural frame is needed behind the panels
options.misconception: believes the floors can hang from the skin, so no structural frame is needed behind it

options.text: The skin to be built without any cavity behind it, since the overlapping joints alone absorb every movement
options.misconception: believes overlapping joints alone absorb all movement, so no cavity is needed behind them

questions.explanation: Because the skin hangs from the frame and carries nothing, the wall can be as thin as the material allows, and it can be light enough to be replaced in parts rather than rebuilt. That is what makes a fully glazed tower possible, and what makes energy performance a matter of the glazing's specification and of the cavity behind it rather than of the wall's thickness. The cavity still matters, for drainage and for insulation, and the overlap exists to shed water. The skin is not a source of heat and not a support of any kind.
questions.hint: Ask which member is carrying the weight of the wall, and what follows for how thick the wall needs to be.

questions.topic: Reading a wall as structure
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a load-bearing wall from a partition on the evidence of a plan
questions.stem: A survey finds that one interior wall runs from the foundations to the roof and sits directly under a line of floor joists, while another wall on the same storey stands on the slab and lines up with no joist at all. How should the two be read?

options.text: The first carries the building and is proportioned for that; the second only divides rooms and can be moved or opened
The first is a party wall marking a boundary, and the second is the structural frame carrying the floors
options.misconception: swaps the terms, calling a boundary wall structural and a frame a partition

options.text: Both are structural, since any vertical wall in a building of this age must by law reach the foundations
options.misconception: assumes every wall in an old building is structural, mistaking age for function

options.text: The second is the earlier wall and the first a later insertion, so the alignment proves the sequence of work
options.misconception: reads alignment as evidence of construction sequence, when it records the floor structure

questions.explanation: Alignment is the evidence. A wall that stands under a line of joists and runs down to a foundation is positioned by the loads it carries, so its thickness and the small size of its openings follow from that job. A wall on the slab that lines up with nothing is a partition: thin, arbitrary in position, and removable without structural consequence. Assuming that every old wall is load-bearing preserves useless fabric and misses the actual structure, while using alignment as a dating tool mistakes a record of the floor construction for a record of the sequence of building.
questions.hint: Ask what sits directly above each wall, and which wall's position was decided by that.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a tall frame resists
questions.learningObjective: identify the loads for which a tall frame needs cores and bracing
questions.stem: A tall tower is stiffened by a core running its full height and by diagonal braces in the outer frame at two levels. What are those members for, as the building sways?

options.text: Lateral loads from wind and from temperature change, taken as tension and compression along a continuous path
The weight of the floors, which the core and the braces carry so that the columns carry nothing at all
options.misconception: thinks the core and braces carry the floors, confusing lateral stability with gravity load

options.text: Movement of the ground, so that the core can hold the tower level while its foundation settles
options.misconception: believes a core can stop ground movement, confusing a superstructure with a foundation

options.text: Air pressure inside the building, so that the skin never has to resist suction from the wind outside
options.misconception: treats the tower as a sealed vessel, so internal pressure loads the skin

questions.explanation: Gravity is the easy case: the columns are sized for the load directly above them, and everything travels straight down. The difficult case is lateral. Wind pressure on a tall elevation grows with the area it catches and with the square of the height, and differential heating makes the frame lean as well, so a slender building both sways and changes shape. A core, braced frame or moment-resisting frame supplies the stiffness that turns that into forces travelling down a defined path into the foundations. None of it concerns the weight of the floors.
questions.hint: Ask which direction the columns are sized for, and which direction the building actually fails to resist.

questions.learningObjective: test a descriptive claim about a structure against how it is built
questions.stem: A visitor centre's publicity describes it as a load-bearing stone building of great mass. A survey finds the walls are a thin stone facing bonded to a reinforced concrete frame. What does the survey do to the claim?

options.text: It removes the load-bearing part of the claim, because the mass is a facing over a frame and carries none of the building
It confirms the claim, since a stone facing still gives the building mass and it still reads as massive
options.misconception: treats visual mass as structural mass, reading an elevation as a load path

options.text: It shows only that the building is of modern construction, leaving the publicity's description of the walls standing
options.misconception: assumes modern construction makes no claims, letting a false description stand

options.text: It shows that the claim is about appearance alone, so the structure behind the facing is beside the point
options.misconception: believes a material claim can be settled by appearance alone

This is why claims about historic buildings are checked against drawings, joints and fabric rather than accepted from a text, and why a survey result that contradicts a published description is a finding about the text as well as about the building. questions.topic: An arch seen in an elevation
questions.learningObjective: read the construction of a cut-stone arch from a described elevation
questions.stem: A close view of an arch shows wedge-shaped stones whose joints all radiate from a point above the opening, an outer ring cut to follow the curve of the face, and one block at the top that is deeper than the rest. What is being shown?

options.text: A cut-stone arch whose voussoirs work in compression on radial joints, with the deepest block closing the ring at the crown
A relieving arch built over a lintel, with the tallest stone set at the crown to spread the weight of the wall above
options.misconception: reads a radiating ring as a flat discharging arch built above a lintel

options.text: A corbelled arch, with each course oversailing the one below it until the courses finally meet at the top
options.misconception: calls it corbelled because the courses narrow, confusing wedge blocks with oversailing courses

options.text: A truss arch, with the tallest block acting as a tie rod between the two springings underneath the curve
options.misconception: thinks the deep crown stone is a tie, importing a truss member into a compression ring

questions.explanation: Radial joints and a wedge shape mean the stones are being squeezed against one another, which is how a compression ring works, and the outer ring cut to the curve is the face of the same voussoirs brought flush. The crown block is both the largest and the last stone set: it closes the ring, and the load arrives there most nearly vertically, so the section needed is greatest there. A relieving arch is a flat discharge above a lintel, corbelling is a sequence of oversailing courses, and a truss needs a straight tie; none of those is what radial joints show.

questions.stem: A measured plan gives a cella of 20 by 30 metres, a free-standing colonnade six columns across the front and thirteen down each flank, and a solid wall closing the rear. What does the plan say about how the building was meant to be seen?

It was entered from one point only, since the solid rear wall proves nothing was meant to be seen from behind

options.misconception: reads a peripteral temple as a covered walk, confusing a viewing colonnade with a commercial one

The cella is a comparatively small box inside that frame, and the blank rear wall is a normal closure of the colonnade, not a sign of alteration. A peripteral temple is not a covered walk, though the two look similar in plan from above.

questions.topic: A section through pendentives
questions.learningObjective: identify the corner surfaces that turn a square bay into a circle
questions.stem: A section through a large dome shows four curved triangular surfaces filling the corners of a square bay, each running from the top of a great arch up to the circle of the dome. What are those four surfaces doing?

options.text: Turning the square bay continuously into a circle, and carrying the dome's load down along the four arches beneath them
Opening the corners of the bay to the light, so that the dome appears to float clear above four separate piers
options.misconception: reads the curved triangles as windows, confusing a load transition with a lighting device

options.text: Propping the dome's base ring outward, since the curves push the circle away from the square it sits on
options.misconception: thinks the pendentives push the base ring outward, reversing which element supplies the support

options.text: Lowering the height of the bay, so a dome of given diameter fits into a room much shallower than it looks
options.misconception: assumes the square bay has been shortened to suit the dome, when the dome sits above its full height

questions.explanation: Those surfaces are pendentives, and their job is a transition and a load path at once. Each is a spherical triangle whose curve runs from the side of the square up to the circle of the dome, so the square is turned into a circle without a step, and the dome's weight is delivered along the four great arches below onto four piers. The reason the effect looks weightless is that the piers are out of sight behind screens, not that the load has gone anywhere. The curves gather force downwards; they never push a base ring outwards.
questions.hint: Ask what shape the corner becomes, and where the weight of the dome finally arrives.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A section through squinches
questions.learningObjective: identify a squinch transition and what it produces
questions.stem: A section shows a square bay whose upper corners are occupied by small arches built across the corner, so an octagon stands inside the square and the dome rests on that octagon. What does the arrangement achieve?

options.text: It turns the square into a circle in steps, carrying the dome on an eight-sided base built up at the corners
It turns the square into a circle in one smooth curve, so the dome rests on a true circle within the square
options.misconception: confuses squinches with pendentives, attributing a continuous curve to a stepped arrangement

options.text: It braces the four walls of the bay, since the corner arches take the outward push of the walls below
options.misconception: reads the corner arches as bracing, confusing a support of the dome with a tie between walls

options.text: It enlarges the bay, since the corner arches carry an upper floor and so widen the room at gallery level
options.misconception: believes the corner arches carry an upper floor, confusing a roof support with a gallery

questions.explanation: Those corner arches are squinches, and they solve the same problem as pendentives by different geometry. Building across each corner cuts the square down to an octagon, and the octagon then receives the circle of the dome, so the transition is a series of steps rather than a smooth curve. The advantage of stepping is that it can be built with the same voussoir technique as the rest of the vault, without setting out a spherical surface. The corner arches carry the dome down; they are not ties between walls and they carry no upper floor.
questions.hint: Ask how many sides the square has after the corners are treated, and how the change of shape happens.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A Palladian villa planned
questions.learningObjective: infer the governing idea of a fourfold villa plan
questions.stem: A plan shows a square central hall with a dome over it, four identical wings on the four sides, each entered by a two-column portico, and a service yard tucked into one corner. What is the plan's governing idea?

options.text: A central principal room held in a symmetrical frame, with subordinate wings and a plan legible from any side
Four separate dwellings of equal standing, since the repetition of the wings marks four owners living on site
options.misconception: reads four repeated wings as four dwellings, ignoring that the parts are unequal in importance

options.text: A fortified square keep, since a square plan with four entrances is the standard plan of a defended house
options.misconception: sees a square plan as fortification, importing a military reading into a country house

options.text: An axial procession, since the corner service yard sets up a processional route straight through the building
options.misconception: assumes a corner service yard implies a processional axis, which the symmetry of the plan denies

questions.explanation: The scheme is a dominant central square with four repeated subordinate units, and the repeat is the point: because no side is privileged, the villa offers four equivalent fronts and all of them converge on the hall in the middle. The porticoes and the dome state the classical vocabulary in domestic form, which is what makes the plan read as architecture and not merely as a house. The single service yard is the one departure from the symmetry, and it is useful precisely because it is confined to a corner and out of the composition.
questions.hint: Ask which room every entrance leads towards, and what four equal wings make impossible about the plan's hierarchy.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Movement through a Baroque interior
questions.learningObjective: infer the intended experience from a described route
questions.stem: A visitor's route is described: a low narrow entrance passage, then a sudden tall oval hall whose long axis lies at an angle to the approach, so that nothing is in view on arrival. What has the sequence been arranged to produce?

options.text: A change of scale and light felt as movement, with the space revealed in stages rather than read at a glance
A larger usable floor area, since an oval hall fits more people into a given width than a rectangle would
options.misconception: believes an oval hall is chosen for floor efficiency, confusing spatial sequence with area

options.text: A direct sightline to the far end, since turning the axis lines the visitor up with the main doorway beyond
options.misconception: thinks a diagonal axis produces a straight sightline, the opposite of what a diagonal denies

options.text: A market hall, since a central room entered from four sides is the traditional shape of a trading floor
options.misconception: reads a central-plan hall as a market, confusing the organisation of movement with its programme

questions.explanation: The sequence is the argument. A low, dim approach is set against a tall, brightly lit, curved space, and the axis is turned so the visitor cannot take the room in at once but must move sideways and around the curve to do it. That converts a single view into an experience unfolding in time, and it is why the plan is organised around circulation rather than about a frontal axis. The same geometry is sometimes used to align a visitor with a distant focus, but here it deliberately removes the alignment that a straight hall would give.
questions.hint: Ask what the visitor can see on arrival, and what the turned axis refuses to show at once.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exposed frame on a tall elevation
questions.learningObjective: interpret an exposed structural frame on a public elevation
questions.stem: An elevation of a tall office building shows a visible lattice of steel columns and diagonal bracing across two faces, with the glass wall set back behind that frame. Why might the frame be left showing like this?

options.text: To make the structural system legible, so that the way the building stands up becomes part of its public face
To admit more daylight, since an exposed frame blocks the sun less than a solid wall on the same elevation
options.misconception: assumes an exposed frame is a daylight measure, confusing structure with shading

options.text: To save the cost of cladding, since leaving the frame bare removes the need for any outer skin at all
options.misconception: believes exposed steel removes the need for a weather skin, when cladding keeps the water out

options.text: To protect the structure from the weather, since bare steel resists weathering better than a faced wall does
options.misconception: thinks bare steel needs no maintenance, when exposed metal in fact corrodes fastest

questions.explanation: Leaving the frame visible is a choice about what the building says: the load path becomes the elevation, and the viewer is shown how the thing stands up. The set-back glazing serves the same legibility, and it also gives the hand that cleans and maintains the facade access to the outer face. None of this is a technical necessity. The frame still needs a skin to keep water out, bare steel is the first thing to corrode, and the bracing and columns occupy floor area whether or not anyone can see them.
questions.hint: Ask what a viewer is being shown, and whether the frame still needs a skin to keep the weather out.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A tripartite palace front
questions.learningObjective: read a graded storey hierarchy on a palace elevation
questions.stem: A palace front has a heavily rusticated ground storey with small barred windows, a principal floor with tall windows and a continuous order of pilasters, and a much lighter top storey. What does that hierarchy express?

options.text: A graded social scale, with the heavy base grounding the house and the lightest storey crowning it
Three separate building campaigns, since the change of material shows one owner's work ending and another's beginning
options.misconception: reads a change of storey as evidence of building campaigns, confusing style with chronology

options.text: A structural necessity, since each storey is heavier than the one above it simply in order to carry the load
options.misconception: believes the storeys differ because of their loads, turning an expressive hierarchy into a structural one

options.text: A military intention, since barred and rusticated walls are built to resist an armed entry from the street
options.misconception: takes barred windows as fortification, ignoring a conventional domestic ground floor

questions.explanation: The three-part front is a convention of the Renaissance palace: a visually massive base, a principal floor given the best light and the largest openings and the formal treatment, and a light attic above. The order running through the upper part binds the whole elevation into one system, so the hierarchy is read as a composition rather than as three separate floors. None of this tracks the structure, and the barred ground-floor windows are a conventional expression of security at the street, not a fortification.
questions.hint: Ask whether the ground floor carries more load than the top, and what the barred windows are really saying.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A Romanesque section measured
questions.learningObjective: read a Romanesque section as a structural argument
questions.stem: A section shows a nave eight metres wide under a barrel vault, a four-metre aisle each side under a quarter-cylinder, and a 1.2-metre wall between them pierced by one narrow window with a deep splayed reveal. What is the section telling you?

options.text: The vault's thrust is taken inside the building, so the thick wall is structural and the window is a small compromise
The wall is thick only to store heat, and the vault needs no support at all from the pier standing beside it
options.misconception: treats thick masonry as insulation, missing that it carries the vault's thrust

options.text: The wall has been thickened by a later addition, since a wall of that thickness cannot be an original medieval build
options.misconception: reads the thickness as evidence of later alteration, when it is the original structural requirement

options.text: The splayed window is structural, since its deep reveal carries the vault's load down into the aisle below
options.misconception: believes a window reveal carries load, confusing a wall's mass with an opening's lining

questions.explanation: The proportions are the argument. An eight-metre span under a barrel vault delivers a real thrust at each springing, and with no exterior supports to receive it that thrust has to be held inside the building, so the walls are thick, continuous and pierced only where the structure can spare the material. The window is a compromise: deep-splayed to let light and thickness in while giving up as little bearing wall as possible. Thick walls of this kind are original to the construction, and a window reveal is an opening, not a support.
questions.hint: Ask where the vault's sideways push is absorbed, and what the wall's thickness therefore has to be.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A Romanesque church measured in plan
questions.learningObjective: interpret measured proportions as a structural argument
questions.stem: A survey of a Romanesque church gives a nave span of 8 m, an aisle of 4 m on each side, a wall between them 1.2 m thick pierced by one window 0.35 m wide, and a barrel vault over the nave. What does the survey establish?

options.text: The vault delivers thrust at the springing, so the thick wall carries it and the small window is a compromise
The wall is 1.2 m thick to hold heat, and the vault's weight passes straight down through it to the ground
options.misconception: treats wall thickness as insulation, missing that it holds the vault's thrust

options.text: The window is deeply splayed to admit as much light as possible, and the wall's thickness is a by-product of that
options.misconception: believes the deep splay is the primary purpose, so the thickness is incidental

options.text: The aisle is a separate structural system, since a half-cylinder roof needs no tie to the wall above it
options.misconception: thinks a half-cylinder aisle roof is structurally independent of the wall above it

questions.explanation: The whole interior is 4 + 1.2 + 8 + 1.2 + 4 = 18.4 m wide, and of that, two walls of 1.2 m are bearing, with only 0.35 m of each given over to an opening. A barrel vault of that span produces a thrust at each springing, and with no exterior prop to receive it, the wall has to be wide and continuous enough to hold itself against being pushed over. The window is then a light source fitted into a structure that can only spare a little material. Reading thickness as insulation misses that the wall is being used as a buttress.
questions.hint: Add up the widths, then ask what the vault is doing to the wall where it springs.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Heights read off a Gothic section
questions.learningObjective: use recorded heights to identify the line of a flying buttress
questions.stem: A section records a nave vault crown 24 m above the floor, an aisle roof at 18 m, and a flyer that springs from an outer pier at 20 m to meet the vault at 19 m. The aisle wall carries nothing but its own weight. What does that show?

options.text: The flyer catches the vault's thrust high up, above the aisle roof, and carries it out to the outer pier
The flyer props the aisle roof, so that the aisle could be vaulted as well as the nave above it
options.misconception: reads the flyer as an aisle prop, confusing an external thrust catcher with a support

options.text: The outer pier is carrying the floor loads of the nave, which is the reason it has to be so tall
options.misconception: believes the outer pier carries the nave's floors, which is why it stands so high

options.text: The vault's thrust is taken at the springing, and the flyer merely stops the aisle wall leaning inwards
options.misconception: thinks the thrust is taken at the springing, leaving the flyer as decoration

questions.explanation: The numbers place the action. The vault's haunch sits at 19 m and its crown at 24 m, the aisle roof is at 18 m, and the flyer meets the vault just above the roof and reaches back to a pier that starts at 20 m. That is exactly the arrangement in which the outward thrust of the vault is intercepted outside and carried down to a separate mass, leaving the aisle wall with nothing to do but stand up. If the thrust were taken at the springing, the wall would have to be thick and the flyer would be pointless.
questions.hint: Compare the height where the flyer meets the vault with the height of the aisle roof.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A clerestory measured bay by bay
questions.learningObjective: infer the structural role of a wall from its measured glazed area
questions.stem: An elevation survey of a clerestory records eight bays, each 4 m wide, each with a window 3.2 m wide and 9 m tall, the piers between them about 0.8 m wide, and the wall 1.2 m thick. What does the record imply about that wall?

options.text: The glass is about four fifths of the bay face, so the wall is a screen and the vault's load bypasses it
The wall is thin because the masons economised, a thin wall being lighter and so stronger than a thick one
options.misconception: believes thin walls are stronger than thick ones, reversing what thickness does in bearing

options.text: The glass is load-bearing, so a 9 m opening can replace a stone pier entirely at that level
options.misconception: treats the glazing as load-bearing, replacing a stone pier with a window

options.text: The windows are a later insertion, since no medieval mason could have cut a 3.2 m opening
options.misconception: assumes no medieval mason could cut an opening that wide, confusing scale with technique

questions.explanation: One bay gives 4 m of width and 3.2 m of it to glass, so roughly four fifths of the visible wall is opening, with the piers left as slender strips. A wall that is mostly hole cannot be doing structural work, and the record says as much: the loads above must be travelling down the piers and out through the buttressing instead. That is exactly what a ribbed vault and a flyer make possible. A load-bearing role is not a matter of taste or of the mason's economy, and an opening of that size is routine in this system.
questions.hint: Compare the width of the window with the width of the bay, and ask what a wall that is mostly hole can carry.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A dome and its drum measured in section
questions.learningObjective: use measured heights to establish what a drum achieves
questions.stem: A section gives a dome 20 m across, its base ring 14 m above the floor, a drum 8 m high pierced by windows 4 m tall, and a square bay 20 m across below with four curved corner surfaces. What does the record establish?

options.text: The 4 m windows sit inside an 8 m drum and so clear the springing, with the ring carried above their heads
A 20 m dome needs a 20 m drum, so the recorded 8 m drum is too short to carry the shell above it
options.misconception: believes a dome's height sets the drum height, mixing up two unrelated dimensions

options.text: The bay below is square, so the dome springs directly from its corners and the drum is redundant
options.misconception: thinks a square bay lets a dome spring straight from the corners, making the drum pointless

options.text: The drum's only function is to admit light, since the dome itself is always lit from the oculus at its crown
options.misconception: believes a dome is always lit from its oculus, ignoring the light the drum admits

questions.explanation: The section says the base ring sits 14 m up and the windows are 4 m tall within a drum that runs from about 8 m to 14 m, so they occupy the lower half of the drum and stop well below the springing. That is the point of the drum: the load-bearing ring is lifted clear of the heads of the openings, so the drum can be a full storey of windows and the wall below is left free of tall holes. The four curved corners below are what turn the square bay into a circle for the ring to sit on; the drum does not replace them.
questions.hint: Locate the base ring against the height of the windows, and count what is happening at the four corners below.
