questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A palace front measured storey by storey
questions.learningObjective: read a measured elevation as evidence of a compositional system
questions.stem: A measured elevation records a ground storey 5 m high in rusticated masonry with 1 m windows, a principal storey 5 m high with 2.5 m windows behind a continuous order of pilasters 1 m wide at 4 m centres, and a 2.5 m attic. What does the record show about the design?

options.text: A 4 m module runs through all three storeys, so one order ties the front into a single system of proportion
Three separate campaigns, since each storey has its own material, its own height and its own window size
options.misconception: reads three storey treatments as three building campaigns, confusing style with date

options.text: A structural hierarchy, since each pilaster carries the storey above and the rustication carries the pilasters
options.misconception: believes pilasters and rustication are structural, turning expression into load path

options.text: An economical scheme, since a 1.2 m module of piers was chosen to use the least dressed stone available
options.misconception: thinks the module was chosen to economise stone, confusing proportion with thrift

questions.explanation: The pilasters sit at 4 m centres and the 4 m bays are the same width, so a single module governs the whole elevation, and the order is continuous rather than repeated storey by storey. That is what makes the front read as one composition instead of three floors. The differences between the storeys, by contrast, are expressive: a heavy base, the largest openings and the formal order on the principal floor, and a light attic. Window size follows social rank, not load, and no part of this scheme is about saving stone.
questions.hint: Compare the bay width with the spacing of the pilasters, and ask which differences track use rather than weight.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The lateral system of a tall tower
questions.learningObjective: interpret a structural survey of a high-rise frame
questions.stem: A survey of a 40-storey tower records a 6 m square concrete core running the full height, perimeter columns at 1.8 m centres, deep outrigger trusses tying core to perimeter at levels 20 and 30, and a solid core plan at every level. What is being described?

options.text: A stiff core tied back to the perimeter at two levels, together resisting sideways wind on the whole envelope
A gravity system, since the core carries every floor load and the perimeter columns are only for the skin
options.misconception: believes the outriggers exist to carry the floors, reversing the lateral and gravity roles

options.text: A cladding system, since the outriggers exist to hang the skin clear of the structure behind it
options.misconception: thinks the trusses hang the cladding, confusing a lateral tie with a fixing

options.text: An isolation system, since the trusses at levels 20 and 30 decouple the tower from its foundation
options.misconception: believes trusses at mid-height decouple the tower, confusing a stiffener with a base isolator

questions.explanation: Wind on a 40-storey elevation is the dominant demand, and the survey shows how it is answered: a core that is stiff in its own plane, and outrigger trusses at two levels that tie the perimeter columns into it so they work with it as a single assembly. The effect is a stiffened tube that carries the lateral load down through the core to the foundations. The columns still carry the floors, the trusses have nothing to do with cladding, and nothing here is decoupled from the ground: the overturning has to be transmitted into it.
questions.hint: Ask which load grows fastest with height, and what the trusses at levels 20 and 30 connect together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Where a vault's thrust is taken
questions.learningObjective: use a report's measurements to locate the thrust path in a thick-walled church
questions.stem: A report states that a church's interior wall is 1.2 m thick, that its windows are 0.35 m wide with deep splayed reveals, and that the nave is covered by a barrel vault. First say where the vault's thrust is being taken, and then say what that implies for the wall.

options.text: Inside the building, in the thick wall itself, so the wall is a bearing mass and the window is a small concession in it
Inside the building, but only because the reveal is splayed, so the deep opening carries the thrust into the aisle
options.misconception: believes a splayed reveal carries thrust, confusing a lining with a buttress

options.text: Nowhere, since a barrel vault is a chain of arches whose outward pushes cancel one another out
options.misconception: thinks adjacent arches cancel each other out, which would need rigid abutments

options.text: Into the aisle roof, which props the vault permanently, so the wall's thickness has nothing to do with the vault
options.misconception: believes an aisle roof can prop a vault permanently, mistaking a temporary prop for structure

questions.explanation: The report describes a building that holds its vaults up from within. A barrel vault is a chain of arches running the length of the nave, and each arch delivers a thrust at its springing; the thrust only cancels if the abutments are rigid, and a wall that is being pushed outwards is not rigid. So the mass of the wall is what holds the vault up, and the opening has to be small because the structure can only spare 0.35 m of it. The splayed reveal admits light and keeps the reveal deep; it carries nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what an arch delivers at its springing, and whether the neighbouring arch can take that force away.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an arch demands of its piers
questions.learningObjective: state the force an arch creates and the resulting demand on its supports
questions.stem: A working drawing shows a semicircular arch of 4 m span springing from two piers 1 m thick, each with a slight batter. First state what the arch does to the load passing over it, and then say what that requires of the piers.

options.text: It turns the load into compression along the ring and delivers an inclined thrust, so each pier must be broad enough not to be pushed over
It turns the load into tension along the ring, so each pier must be slender and light so the arch can draw it inwards
options.misconception: believes an arch puts its supports in tension, reversing the load path

options.text: It removes the load from the piers altogether, so they are needed only to hold the stones of the ring in place
options.misconception: thinks an arch unloads its supports, when the thrust is precisely the load they take

options.text: It doubles the load on each pier, so a pier under an arch must be twice the strength of one under a lintel
options.misconception: believes an arch doubles the load, confusing a different force with a larger one

questions.explanation: An arch is a compression ring, and the force it delivers at each springing is inclined: part down, part sideways outwards. That sideways component is the demand, and it is answered by mass and by width at the base, which is why piers under arches are broad, battered and often buttressed further out, and why an arch cannot stand on a slender support. The ring does not unload the supports, it redirects the load into them at a different angle, and it does not multiply the weight either.
questions.hint: Ask which way the force leans as it leaves the ring at its springing, and what resists a sideways push at a pier's foot.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The corner transition under a dome
questions.learningObjective: state the geometry a pendentive solves and the alternative solution
questions.stem: A section shows a dome carried on four curved triangular surfaces that rise from the tops of four great arches to meet the circle of the dome directly. First say what geometry those surfaces solve, and then say what the alternative construction would be.

options.text: They turn a square bay into a circle continuously; the alternative builds small arches across the corners to make an octagon first
They turn a circle into a square so the dome has a flat base; the alternative is to cut the dome down to fit the bay
options.misconception: reads the pendentives as squaring a circle, reversing the direction of the transition

options.text: They hold up a drum above the dome, so its weight is carried upwards; the alternative is a ring beam under the shell
options.misconception: thinks a dome can be carried from above, which changes nothing about where its weight goes

options.text: They light the four corners of the bay in place of windows; the alternative is a clerestory below the springing
options.misconception: confuses a load transition with a source of light

questions.explanation: The four surfaces are pendentives, and the problem they solve is a mismatch of geometry: a square bay has four corners, a circle has none, and something has to close the difference. Pendentives close it in one continuous curve from the sides of the square up to the circle, gathering the load along the four great arches. The alternative is the squinch, which closes each corner with a small arch or corbelled mass, turning the square into an octagon before the circle arrives. Neither device lifts anything, and neither is a source of light.
questions.hint: Count the corners of the bay and the corners of a circle, and ask how the gap can be closed smoothly or in steps.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a survey of a frame reveals
questions.learningObjective: use the position of walls and cores to state the structural system
questions.stem: A survey of a modern tower finds that every exterior wall stands on the floor slabs and lines up with no beam, while a concrete core runs the full height and continues below the lowest floor. First say what the core is doing, and then say what the walls' position shows.

options.text: The core carries the building and resists sideways load, and the walls' position shows that a frame carries every load
The core is only a lift shaft, and the walls' position shows the frame is redundant since nothing lines up at all
options.misconception: assumes a core is only for lifts and services, ignoring its structural work

options.text: The core is decorative, and the walls' position shows that this is really a load-bearing masonry building in disguise
options.misconception: claims a frame has no structure at all, which the survey contradicts

options.text: The core carries the lifts and the services, and the walls' position shows their earlier positions were accidental
options.misconception: treats the absence of alignment as accident rather than as the point of a frame

questions.explanation: A core that runs past the lowest floor is founded and continuous, and a core that size is placed there to take load: the gravity of the floors and services in it, and the building's resistance to sideways movement. Meanwhile the exterior walls line up with nothing because nothing depends on them; a frame lets the wall sit wherever the plan requires. That combination, a stiff core plus an independent skin, is what a tall framed building is. It does not mean there is no structure, and it is not a lift shaft by itself.
questions.hint: Ask what runs below the lowest floor, and what would happen if a wall were moved a metre to the left.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The load path out through a Gothic choir
questions.learningObjective: sequence the members along a vault's route to the ground
questions.stem: Trace the route a vault's load takes in a Gothic choir, from the ceiling surface to the ground, putting these four stages in the order they must occur.

options.text: The outer buttress pier takes the thrust down through its own mass into the foundations
The vault web carries its own weight to the diagonal and transverse ribs spanning between the piers
The ribs gather that weight and deliver concentrated thrusts onto the compound piers inside the church
The flyer receives the thrust above the aisle roof and passes it outward to the outer pier

questions.explanation: The order is fixed by contact, since each member can only hand on what it has already received. The web is the first to feel the load and it spans only from rib to rib, so it passes everything to the ribs. The ribs, which are much heavier members, gather it and deliver it in a few concentrated places, which is why the piers inside are compound and why the wall between them can be opened. The thrust at the haunch is then caught outside by the flyer, which passes it over the aisle roof to the outer pier, and the pier's own mass takes it into the ground.
questions.hint: Ask which member touches which, and follow the load from the ceiling surface downwards.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of building a stone arch
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of raising a masonry arch
questions.stem: A mason is about to raise a semicircular stone arch between two piers, working without a crane and with no metal available. Put these four stages in the order in which they must happen.

options.text: Strike the timber centring once the ring is closed and the joints at the crown are wedged tight
Set out the centre line and build the two abutments up to the springing of the arch
Lay the voussoirs in courses from both springings, working upwards towards the crown
Erect the timber centring that will carry the voussoirs until the ring is closed

questions.explanation: Each stage depends on the state left by the one before it. Nothing can be set out before the supports exist, so the abutments are built to the springing first. The voussoirs cannot be laid without something to hold them, because a half-built ring of loose wedges would fall, so the timber centring goes up next. The courses then rise symmetrically from both springings, which keeps the ring balanced and avoids overloading one side while it is open. Only when the last joint is closed can the centring be struck.
questions.hint: Ask what each stage needs to be already in place, and which one would collapse if the previous one were missing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Investigating a tower that has settled
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a structural investigation and repair
questions.stem: A tall masonry tower has been leaning for a century and its base is visibly distorted where the ground has given way. Put these four stages of work in the order in which they must be done.

options.text: Design an intervention that acts at the place where the load has proved to be unbalanced
Survey the tower, measure the lean, and record which courses have opened and where
Carry the work out in stages, re-measuring the lean after each one before continuing
Establish where the load is unbalanced, which in a settled tower means its base and not its top

questions.explanation: The sequence is forced by what a builder needs to know before acting. Measurement comes first and does double duty: it tells you what is happening and it sets the baseline against which any later movement will be judged. Only then can the cause be identified, and in a settled tower the cause is in the base, because the lean is a symptom of an unbalanced load path rather than a fault of the upper courses. The repair has to act there, and it has to be staged, since changing a foundation can move the building further before it settles back.
questions.hint: Ask what you need to know before choosing a fix, and whether the top or the foot is where the problem is.

questions.topic: The order of erecting a classical temple
questions.learningObjective: sequence the main stages of erecting a post-and-lintel temple
questions.stem: A classical temple is being built in stone, with columns, an architrave, a frieze and a pediment. Put these four main stages in the order in which they must be carried out.

options.text: Set the pediment above the level of the frieze, its raking cornices following the roof's slope
Raise the columns on the stylobate, correcting their heights before any of them is fixed
Lay the stylobate, the levelled platform on which the whole colonnade will stand
Set the architrave on the capitals, tying the tops of the columns into one continuous member

questions.explanation: The order is a matter of what each stage rests on. The stylobate comes first because everything else is positioned from it and because a colonnade standing on an uneven platform will run visibly out of true. The columns follow, all brought to the same height before any of them is fixed, so that the architrave can be a level continuous beam. The entablature is then laid on the capitals, and the pediment is the last thing, because it has to meet the top of the frieze at a single level and close the front as a finished composition.
questions.hint: Ask what each stage stands on, and which one has to wait for the level of the course beneath it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a wall came to be mostly window
questions.learningObjective: explain the structural chain that frees a church wall for glass
questions.stem: Explain how it became possible for the wall of a medieval church to be mostly window while a stone vault still stands above it. Give the chain of causes, not a list of parts.

answer.exemplar: The chain runs from the arch outwards, and every step is forced by the previous one. A stone vault is a series of arches, and an arch loads its supports in two directions at once: down, and outwards at the springing. That outward component is called thrust, and it will push a wall over unless something receives it. There are only two places it can go. Either it is held inside the building, in which case the walls must be massive, continuous and pierced as little as possible, which is exactly the thick-walled church with small windows; or it is taken outside, in which case the wall between the piers is no longer a bearing mass. Taking it outside is what a buttress does, and the flying buttress does it better: a half-arch is carried from a heavy outer pier over the roof of the aisle and meets the vault high up, near the haunch, where the thrust is strongest and where a low prop could not reach. The second move is to concentrate the load. A ribbed vault is not a solid ceiling but a framework of ribs with thin webs slung between them, so the ribs gather the web's weight and deliver it in a few places onto piers instead of along a whole wall. Once the thrust is outside and the load arrives at points, the wall between the piers has no structural job: it is a windscreen. It can be built thin and opened as widely as the stone bars and mullions allow, and those bars carry the weight of the glass, which is why the tracery is a structure of its own. What has not happened is that the loads disappeared. The thrust has been moved from the wall to the outer pier, the weight has been gathered onto piers, and the wall has been freed. A weak answer lists the flying buttress, the rib vault and the pointed arch and stops there, without saying what force each one deals with or why the order of the chain matters.

questions.explanation: A full answer gives the chain in causal order: thrust at the springing, thrust taken outside by the flyer, load concentrated onto piers by the ribs, wall freed, wall opened. It names the force at each step and says where the force has gone, and it is explicit that the thrust has been relocated rather than abolished. A weak response lists the components without the force, or stops at the pointed arch as though the arch itself did the work.
questions.hint: Start with the force a vault produces at its springing, and follow where that force is made to go.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why an arch beats a lintel, and what it costs
questions.learningObjective: explain the physical advantage of an arch and the price paid for it
questions.stem: Explain why an arch of a given span can carry so much more load than a straight stone lintel of the same span, and why the builders of a stone building could not simply use arches everywhere.

answer.exemplar: The advantage comes down to how stone behaves. A lintel is a beam: held at both ends and loaded along its length, it bends, and bending puts the top of the section in compression and the bottom in tension. Stone is excellent in compression and very poor in tension, so the crack starts on the underside and runs across the member. Worse, the bending moment at midspan grows with the square of the span, so doubling the opening multiplies the bending demand by roughly four, and a limestone lintel is limited to a modest width no matter how deep it is. An arch never asks for that. A ring of wedge-shaped blocks, with its joints cut radial so the thrust runs across them at right angles, is squeezed against itself, and masonry is strongest exactly in compression. The arch can therefore be wide while its individual stones stay small enough to quarry, to lift and to bed. The price is the same physics seen from the other side. The load has not been abolished, it has been redirected: a semicircular arch delivers at each springing a force that is inclined outward as well as down, and something has to receive that thrust. The supports must be broad, heavy and often battered, and where the arch stands above a lower space the thrust must be carried further out to an external pier, which is why arched buildings are full of buttress masses. An arch is also generally heavier than the wall it replaces, since a void has to be filled with a ring of stone, and it cannot be built without temporary support: a timber centring has to hold the voussoirs until the keystone closes the ring at the crown. So arches are the answer where wide openings and heavy loads meet, and walls stay straight where the span is short, the material is timber, or the supports could not take a thrust.

questions.explanation: A full answer names bending and the tension it produces, ties the limit on span to the growth of the bending moment, then explains the arch as a compression ring, and finally accounts for the price: thrust at the springings, massive supports, extra weight, and the need for centring. A weak response says only that arches are stronger, or explains the arch without ever mentioning the tension that breaks the lintel.
questions.hint: Ask what the underside of a loaded lintel is doing, and what the arch's supports have to take instead.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why Greek and Roman temples are planned differently
questions.learningObjective: relate a temple plan to its ritual and to its structure
questions.stem: Explain why a Greek temple and a Roman temple are planned so differently, and how each plan suits the act carried out in it. Deal with both the ritual and the construction.

answer.exemplar: The two plans answer two different rituals, and each ritual brought its own structure with it. The Greek temple is a peripteral building: a free-standing colonnade runs down both flanks and across the rear, with a porch on one short side, so the same order and entablature face every direction and the building is composed to be looked at from outside. The act is a procession that goes round the temenos, not a single ceremony at a single door, and the architecture is a continuous surface to be walked along. The structure is post-and-lintel: stone columns, a stone architrave, a pediment, with a relatively small cella inside, because long stone lintels cannot span far and the cella therefore has to be modest. The Roman temple turns that inside out. It stands on a high podium reached by one wide staircase at the front, with no steps on the other sides, so the approach and the view are concentrated on a single axis, and the ritual takes place in front of the deity's image at the far end of it. That is possible partly because of the podium, which gives the building a platform on which the cella can be roofed with concrete vaults carried on piers, so the interior is much larger and the front can be a screen of columns rather than a load-bearing wall, with an engaged order or a pseudoperteral colonnade standing against the cella instead of free in front of it. The two are therefore not a better and a worse version of one idea. One is an equal-sided object to be walked around, built of beams, for a rite of circumambulation; the other is a focused axis ending in an image, built of vaults on a platform, for a single approach and a single ceremony. A weak answer describes the shapes without the rites, or the rites without noticing that the vault and the podium are what make the larger Roman cella possible.

questions.explanation: A full answer links plan to ritual and plan to structure, and shows that the two are connected: the podium is what allows the vaulted, larger cella, and the cella's size is a consequence of the construction. It explains the peripteral colonnade as a surface for circumambulation and the single stair as a focused axis. A weak response lists features on each side and never says what the building was for.
questions.hint: Ask how many ways in each building has, what the visitor does at the door, and how large the inner room can be.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a steel frame changed, and what it did not
questions.learningObjective: evaluate what a new structural system changed and what it left unresolved
questions.stem: Explain what a steel frame changed about the limits on building height, and what it left unchanged. Do not treat the change as an unmixed gain.

answer.exemplar: What the frame changed is the relationship between the building and its walls. In a load-bearing masonry building the wall is a continuous vertical member whose thickness is set by the loads it takes, so the more storeys there are, the more massive and the more inarticulate the supports become, and windows are limited by what the wall can spare. A frame takes the gravity load instead: columns on a grid carry the floors straight down to the foundations, and the exterior wall becomes a skin hung on the outside of that grid. Once the wall is freed, the whole upper part of the elevation can be glass, the plan can be opened up, and the interior can be rearranged without touching a bearing wall, and the building's weight is concentrated on a few points rather than spread along its length. Height stops being a question of stacking heavier and heavier walls. What the frame did not change is that buildings still have to stand up against sideways movement. Wind pressure on a tall elevation grows with the area exposed and with the height, and a slender frame behaves like a mast, so above a certain height the governing problem is sway and the acceleration it causes, not the strength of the columns. That is why cores, braced frames, outrigger trusses and moment-resisting connections appear as height rises, and why a tall building is often a stiffened tube rather than a stack of frames. Three further problems are untouched as well. The foundations still have to take the whole weight and now also the overturning, concentrated into a smaller area. Fire is a new and often worse problem, since steel loses strength quickly and a frame means larger open floors. And the frame does not make a building cheap: it replaces one set of costs, foundations, steel and fire protection, with another. The honest account is a change in which load the walls carry, bought at the price of a new problem in lateral stiffness and a new problem in fire.

questions.explanation: A full answer identifies the transfer of load from continuous walls to a column grid, and then names at least one problem the frame did not solve, such as wind sway, foundation demand or fire, and says why it got worse. A weak response celebrates the frame as a pure gain, or lists limitations without connecting them to what the frame actually changed.
questions.hint: Ask which member the load moved into, and then ask what force grows fastest as the building gets taller.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Corners closed to carry a dome
questions.learningObjective: count the pendentives needed to turn a square bay into a circle
questions.stem: A circular dome is to rest directly on a square bay, with no drum and no squinches. Each corner of the square must be closed by one continuous curved triangular surface. How many such surfaces does the geometry require?
questions.explanation: The count follows from the mismatch. A square has four corners and a circle has none, so every corner has to be closed, and each closure has to carry load continuously from the square's sides up to the circle of the dome. One surface does one corner, so four are required, and they correspond to the four great arches on the sides of the bay, which is why a building with pendentives has four piers rather than a ring of columns. Fewer surfaces would leave a corner open and the dome would have nothing to bear on at that point; more would be redundant, since there are only four corners to close.
questions.hint: Count the corners of the square and the corners of a circle, and remember what each closure has to do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Ribs and webs in a quadripartite vault
questions.learningObjective: count the diagonal ribs in a vault divided into four webs
questions.stem: A quadripartite rib vault is divided into four curved webs. How many diagonal ribs run corner to corner across the bay, counting only the diagonals and not the transverse ribs that cross from side to side?
questions.explanation: The relationship is arithmetic: each diagonal rib, together with the boundary ribs, encloses a pair of webs, so a vault of n diagonal ribs has twice as many severies as ribs. Four webs therefore means two diagonals, and those two diagonals cross at the crown, which is why the quadripartite vault is the standard form over a square bay. The other ribs in the vault are not diagonals: the transverse ribs cross the bay from side to side at the ends, the formerets run parallel to the wall, and a longitudinal ridge rib may be added along the axis. Counting all of them together would give a different and wrong answer.
questions.hint: Draw the bay as a square and see how many webs one diagonal cuts it into.
